A.explanation: Dividing $30 \, \Omega$ by 3 is wrong because longer length increases resistance and smaller area also increases it.

B.explanation: Resistance cannot stay at $30 \, \Omega$ because both length and cross-sectional area change when the wire is redrawn.

C.explanation: Multiplying by 3 alone gives $90 \, \Omega$ but it ignores that the same mass and triple length force the area to become one-third.

D.explanation: Triple length and one-third area give a factor of $3 \times 3 = 9$, so $9 \times 30 \, \Omega = 270 \, \Omega$.

hints: Notice the second wire has three times the length but the same mass and same material, so its volume $AL$ must stay the same.
Recall $R = \rho L / A$ with the same resistivity $\rho$, so a larger $L$ increases $R$ while a smaller $A$ increases $R$ further.
First find the new area from $A_1L_1 = A_2L_2$ with $L_2 = 3L_1$, then form the ratio $R_2/R_1$ to get the numerical resistance in $\Omega$.
walkthrough: Write the data: $R_1 = 30 \, \Omega$, $L_2 = 3L_1$, same resistivity $\rho$ and same density because it is the same material.
Use $R = \rho L / A$ for each wire, so $R_1 = \rho L_1 / A_1$ and $R_2 = \rho L_2 / A_2$.
Use constant volume from constant mass: $A_1L_1 = A_2L_2$. With $L_2 = 3L_1$, then $A_2 = A_1L_1 / 3L_1 = A_1/3$.
Calculate $R_2 = 9 \times 30 \, \Omega = 270 \, \Omega$, which has the correct resistance unit. This is option D.
